chapter: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
title: Merging the black and white musicians' unions
summary: Royal discusses the long fight to merge Local 767 into Local 47, officers, his father's union presidency and why 47 needed the money.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Buddy told me that even though he had a job, the -- I guess it was contractors? Whoever it was that was in charge of (inaudible).
Yes, the contractor is the guy that is the contractor now for Motown.
Well, Buddy said the man in charge of doing the paperwork refused to make out his paycheck because he said he didn't know how to handle the deductions for _______.
That's right.
And Buddy says the difficulty that he had in that band was the beginnings, at least in his mind, of the thought that we got to get one union in this town, instead of two.
Not really. There had been a whole lot done before that. It wasn't his --
I guess that was when Buddy got involved.
That was when he got involved, because Buddy was just a young man at that time. He was in his early 20s and there had been other fellows that had worked out there

and they knew how to take care of the breaking down of the payrolls, because at that time, I was the Vice President of the black union. So, they knew how to do it. The only thing is somebody was trying to give him a bad time.
Well, he realized that.

Somebody was using that as an excuse, which usually was the thing. But that -- there was a whole lot of guys that worked toward the amalgamation of the two unions and it went on for many, many years. As a matter of fact --
(Inaudible) effort start?
The effort started way back in the '20s, but it was not allowed because they had some dudes up ahead of the national there that wouldn't go for it.
Buddy said that Patrillo (PHONETIC) was against it all the way.

Patrillo was against it and the man before him was against it. There was another old Dutchman was ahead of -- by the name of Webber, that was before Patrillo, and they were all against it. My father was one of the past presidents of the musician's union, way back around 1921.
(Inaudible)?

Oh, I don't know. Way back around 1918, '19, '20, somewhere around there. My father was one of the first presidents. But it had to be a whole lot of things to happen before this union could become one.
Well, 47, the majority (inaudible).
They didn't want it either.
They figured (inaudible).

They didn't want it, either. One of the main reasons why, at the particular time that Local 767 went into 47 and were accepted was that Local 47 had bought a new building and they was fixing to go bankrupt and we had a little money over there and we actually helped them out by putting our little money into their coffers and going and it opened their eyes a little bit more, because we had a building to sell and we had several thousands in our accounts. We had several hundred good-paying people to come in and it helped them out. They needed us at that particular time.
I was away on the road with the Basie Band at the time that they came together, but I was sort of up to what was happening at the time.
Who were the member of the 47 that were helped, do you know?
Well, a lot of that came on the hands of -- Benny Carter was one of the guys that was forwarding that movement and Mac Morrel Young (PHONETIC) and a few other people --
(Inaudible).
They were in 767.
(Inaudible) among the leaders (inaudible).
That's correct. They were --
They had a few friends in 47, didn't they?
Oh, there were a whole lot of friends down there. Now, they would have to be the ones to tell you who their particular friends were, because I wouldn't know.
